incidents.vector: An internal business system was inadvertently moved outside a VPN-restricted network during a migration in February 2025, leaving it externally accessible; an unauthorized account was later created and used to access the system.
incidents.impact: An outside party accessed a database starting June 27, 2026 containing customer names, business emails, phone numbers and identity documents (driver's licenses, passports, utility bills); DigiCert's certificate-issuance systems and customer login credentials were not affected.

incidents.vector: An external actor used offensive "agentic" AI techniques to gain unauthorized access to internal tools; a separate on-path attack intercepted some customer passwords in transit.
incidents.impact: Names, usernames, password hashes and live authentication tokens were exposed for all Chainalysis users, who include law enforcement, national security and crypto-industry customers; the company took its KYT, Reactor and other investigative products offline amid an ongoing multifront incident.

incidents.victim: Multiple organizations (unnamed) via exposed cloud credentials
incidents.vector: A Chinese-linked group used an AI-driven agentic offensive framework ("ARTEX"), paired with the DeepSeek LLM and a second commercial model, to scan public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, then pivoted compromised multitenant application credentials into cloud resource discovery and data exfiltration.
incidents.impact: In one case an AI agent went from scanning GitHub to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes; a compromised vendor-owned multitenant application credential was used to access multiple downstream customer tenants, with further exfiltration from Azure Key Vaults and Storage Accounts as part of a broader espionage campaign against multiple targets.

incidents.victim: Thousands of iPhone and Android users (US, Ukraine, and other mixed targets)
incidents.vector: A Russian state-linked espionage group compromised legitimate websites (including via a supply-chain compromise of Ukrainian analytics firm Plerdy) and stood up lookalike domains to serve device-fingerprinting JavaScript to mobile visitors, then delivered one of three exploit chains targeting unpatched iOS or Android vulnerabilities to selected victims.
incidents.impact: A weeklong watering-hole campaign exposed potentially thousands of mobile users to fingerprinting and exploit delivery; confirmed compromised sites included a US chemical-industry trade association, a Ukrainian gas producer, a Bulgarian military-linked organization and an Australian medical clinic.

incidents.vector: A ransomware gang encrypted systems across the library network; the initial access method has not been disclosed.
incidents.impact: WiFi, on-site computers, checkout/return machines, digital media services and the mobile app were taken down across all 66 branches serving 2.3 million Queens residents; no gang had claimed credit as of Thursday evening.

incidents.vector: Extortionists email small game studios threatening to use AI tools to clone their public demos or unreleased games and publish them first unless a ransom is paid.
incidents.impact: Demanded fees have ranged from hundreds to thousands of US dollars; the campaign is believed to be the main reason a large number of developers pulled demos from Steam in recent weeks.

incidents.victim: Supermarket chains and blood banks across Europe (France, Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden); suspected link to US military commissary incidents
incidents.attacker: Unknown — claimed by pro-Russian hacktivist groups (claims disputed by researchers)
incidents.vector: Attackers exploited internet-accessible industrial refrigeration and cold-chain controllers (Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC, Dixell and Copeland XWEB systems), many protected only by default credentials, to force units into continuous defrost/heating cycles.
incidents.impact: Hundreds of supermarkets across at least 10 EU countries were hit in successive waves starting Oct 11, with over 40 Ahold Delhaize-owned stores affected in the latest wave; tens of millions of euros/dollars in spoiled inventory and equipment damage, some fires reported, and an attempted attack on three French national blood bank refrigeration units was caught and stopped before plasma was damaged. CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, DOT and ENISA issued joint hardening advisories.

incidents.victim: Amadeus IT Group, with downstream exposure at Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, Asiana Airlines, Singapore Airlines and Malaysia Airlines
incidents.vector: Attackers used credentials assigned to a system account to exploit a vulnerability in Amadeus's travel-booking display environment; Amadeus has not detailed how the credentials were obtained.
incidents.impact: Japan Airlines reported 92,000 affected customers, Singapore Airlines 46,000 records and Cathay Pacific 53,000 records; exposed data included booking numbers, passenger names, flight details and in some cases passport and frequent-flyer information. Amadeus says there is no evidence payment data was taken and has since patched the vulnerability.

incidents.vector: An attacker used privilege-escalation tools (GodPotato, SeImpersonate) and the Impacket library to reach the agency's databases and copy SQL Server backups to a staging server hosted in Singapore.
incidents.impact: 27 backup databases totaling roughly 69GB — covering overseas-employment case management, contracts, and cashier/bank records — were exfiltrated in just 24 minutes; the data has not yet been seen for sale, and attribution to a nation-state or cybercriminal group remains unconfirmed.

incidents.attacker: Russia — state-linked espionage group (Belarusian government-linked proxy)
incidents.vector: A Belarusian government-linked group conducted its first-ever destructive data-wiping attack.
incidents.impact: The wiping attack hit a Ukrainian manufacturer with an important role in the country's transportation sector, marking a notable escalation from this actor's typical espionage and influence operations, per ESET's Q2-Q3 APT activity report.
Hackers stole approximately $49 million in crypto assets from Brazil's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

incidents.victim: Li Auto EV owners in Russia
incidents.vector: Attackers used leaked vehicle identification numbers to find expired eSender eSIM numbers tied to Li Auto master accounts, re-registered the eSIMs and re-registered the cars to new accounts, generating a new master digital key.
incidents.impact: At least 20 confirmed owners were locked out of their vehicles' doors and engines in this second wave of attacks (after a first wave in July of last year); attackers now demand roughly $500-$600 per vehicle to restore access, down from over $3,000 previously. Li Auto says it is working on a fix that removes the Chinese-phone-number dependency.

incidents.victim: At least four U.S. universities (New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, Massachusetts)
incidents.vector: Two Canadian nationals allegedly stole credentials and deployed rootkits and cryptomining malware on compromised university systems, including a supercomputer, using rented VPS infrastructure registered under false identities.
incidents.impact: Historic intrusions (2016-2019) commandeered significant processing power, including at least one supercomputer, for unauthorized cryptocurrency mining; one defendant was extradited to the US on Oct. 28 and arraigned this week, facing up to 10 years in prison.

incidents.vector: An attacker used stolen credentials to access the update servers for cPGuard, an anti-malware product for cPanel and shared-hosting servers, and pushed a malicious update.
incidents.impact: cPGuard versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19, delivered on Nov. 2, collected /etc/shadow files, MySQL configuration, root shell history and SSH files from affected servers; the vendor released a clean version (5.88.25) and urged credential rotation.

incidents.vector: A North Korean state-sponsored hacking group ran a multi-stage social-engineering campaign: a malicious Homebrew install compromised one engineer, then a fake job-interview process with a trojanized coding test compromised a second engineer, after which an internal AI tool was abused to escalate access to two additional Wallet engineers' systems.
incidents.impact: Attackers stole tokens across 11 cryptocurrencies worth $6.3 billion — the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, surpassing the $1.46 billion Bybit hack. Binance covered 95% of losses from its own reserves and helped freeze about $2.8 billion of the stolen stablecoins; roughly $3.25 billion, mostly in Bitcoin and Ethereum, remains unrecovered and is still being laundered.
